screens.title: How you'll validate skills
screens.narratorSegment: Knowing what to implement is only half the work. This second objectives screen focuses on validating and debugging your movement. You'll test that AddMovementInput produces expected motion by confirming the pawn moves relative to the controller's yaw, and not the world's fixed axes, unless intentionally implemented for a top-down design. You'll check that Look input updates controller rotation and that inverted mouse Y behavior comes from input mapping decisions rather than code. For troubleshooting, learn to reproduce frame-rate variation: simulate a low frame environment and observe whether movement scales correctly — if it doesn't, the fix is to multiply by GetWorld()->GetDeltaSeconds(). Also watch for movement that ignores collision: that usually means no movement component processed the input. Finally, practice tuning MovementSpeed and the movement component's MaxSpeed while watching for tunneling at very high speeds. These validation steps help you move from code changes to a playable, robust pawn.

screens.title: APawn and AController: roles and relationship
screens.narratorSegment: Start by understanding the division of responsibilities between APawn and AController. The pawn is the in-world actor that can move and collide, but by default it lacks higher-level intent; the controller — often a player controller — provides that intent and the view orientation. GetControlRotation on the controller returns where the player is looking in world space. When we want movement that feels natural to the player, we derive a yaw-only rotation from the controller so the pawn's forward and right directions align with the player's facing direction. This prevents awkward movement where forward on the keyboard moves the pawn in a different direction than the camera. A concrete example: if a player looks 45 degrees right and presses forward, using the controller yaw makes the pawn move toward that 45-degree heading. A common misconception is assuming the pawn's actor rotation always matches the camera. Instead, the controller can be rotated independently; the pawn only follows if you enable bUseControllerRotationYaw or respond to controller rotation explicitly. Takeaway: treat the controller as the source of viewpoint and use its yaw to compute movement axes for player-centric motion.

Definition card
Key definition

AController provides possession and viewpoint. GetControlRotation returns the controller's world rotation; use its yaw to derive directional vectors for intuitive player movement.

Concrete example

screens.title: AddMovementInput: parameters and behavior
screens.narratorSegment: AddMovementInput is the recommended way to request motion from a pawn. Conceptually, it doesn't instantly teleport the pawn; instead it queues a directional request that a movement component will process. The two main parameters are a world-space FVector direction and a float scale. The direction is typically a unit forward or right vector derived from the controller yaw; the scale comes from your input axis value multiplied by a MovementSpeed and crucially by the frame delta. A concrete example: when the player presses the forward key, the Move function calls AddMovementInput with the derived forward vector and a scale of InputY times MovementSpeed times GetWorld()->GetDeltaSeconds(). A common mistake is to pass raw speed without delta seconds, which ties movement to frame rate. Another pitfall is calling SetActorLocation inside Move — that bypasses collision handling. The right approach is to ensure a UFloatingPawnMovement or character movement component exists to process the queued inputs so sliding and collision work as expected. Takeaway: treat AddMovementInput as a request, and pair it with a movement component. AddMovementInput: parameters and behavior means it queues movement requests processed by a movement component; always scale by delta seconds for consistent motion.. In practical terms, how the function accumulates movement and works with components. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Process
AddMovementInput mechanics
Queue a directional request that movement components honor.
API pattern
// Move (conceptual scale uses delta seconds)
AddMovementInput(ForwardDirection, InputY * MovementSpeed * GetWorld()->GetDeltaSeconds());
AddMovementInput(RightDirection,   InputX * MovementSpeed * GetWorld()->GetDeltaSeconds());
Remember: direction should be a unit vector and scale drives how far the pawn should move this frame. The movement component may normalize or combine multiple requests before applying velocity and collision.
Explanation bullets
  • It accumulates inputs each frame — call it whenever you have input.
  • Movement components process the accumulated inputs, performing sliding and collision response.
  • Scale by GetWorld()->GetDeltaSeconds() for frame-rate independence.
  • Do not use SetActorLocation in input handlers; it bypasses physics and collision.
Concrete scenario
Pressing forward while looking down a corridor should produce smooth forward motion and sliding off small obstacles if a movement component handles the input.

Treat AddMovementInput as a per-frame request; pair it with UFloatingPawnMovement or a proper movement component and scale by delta seconds.

keyIdea.text: Derive yaw-only forward/right from controller rotation and call AddMovementInput with input axes scaled by MovementSpeed and delta seconds.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
Move function (C++)
Full snippet
// In AMyPlayerPawn.cpp, within the Move function:
void AMyPlayerPawn::Move(const FInputActionValue& Value)
{
  FVector2D MovementVector = Value.Get<FVector2D>();

  if (Controller && (MovementVector.X != 0.0f || MovementVector.Y != 0.0f))
  {
    const FRotator Rotation = Controller->GetControlRotation();
    const FRotator YawRotation(0, Rotation.Yaw, 0);

    const FVector ForwardDirection = FRotationMatrix(YawRotation).GetUnitAxis(EAxis::X);
    const FVector RightDirection   = FRotationMatrix(YawRotation).GetUnitAxis(EAxis::Y);

    AddMovementInput(ForwardDirection, MovementVector.Y * MovementSpeed * GetWorld()->GetDeltaSeconds());
    AddMovementInput(RightDirection,   MovementVector.X * MovementSpeed * GetWorld()->GetDeltaSeconds());
  }
}
Explanation
  • Value.Get returns the input vector from your input action mapping.
  • Controller validity prevents null dereferences when possession is not active.
  • YawRotation strips pitch and roll so movement stays on the horizontal plane.
  • Multiplying by MovementSpeed and delta seconds makes motion consistent across machines.
Example
Holding right moves the pawn along the right unit vector derived from controller yaw, scaled to MovementSpeed units per second.

screens.title: Implementing Look: yaw and pitch control
screens.narratorSegment: Camera look is implemented by forwarding mouse or stick input to the controller via AddControllerYawInput and AddControllerPitchInput. These functions change the controller's rotation incrementally, which in turn affects the pawn's orientation if your pawn is set to use controller rotation for yaw or if you read the controller rotation for movement. The Look function should extract a FVector2D look axis from the input action, test controller validity, and call the two functions with the provided X and Y input values. A real example: moving the mouse to the right produces a positive X value; calling AddControllerYawInput with that value rotates the controller right. The chapter mentions negating mouse Y for an inverted look setup, which is controlled via the input mapping rather than code; if your mapping inverts Mouse Y, you do not need to negate again in code. A common mistake is applying pitch directly to the pawn without clamping, which can lead to the camera flipping over. Use your input mapping and spring arm settings to handle clamping and inversion. Final takeaway: keep look input simple — pass values to controller functions and manage inversion in mappings.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
Look function (C++)
Forward input deltas to the controller to rotate view.
Full snippet
// In AMyPlayerPawn.cpp, within the Look function:
void AMyPlayerPawn::Look(const FInputActionValue& Value)
{
  FVector2D LookAxisVector = Value.Get<FVector2D>();

  if (Controller && (LookAxisVector.X != 0.0f || LookAxisVector.Y != 0.0f))
  {
    AddControllerYawInput(LookAxisVector.X);
    AddControllerPitchInput(LookAxisVector.Y);
  }
}
Practical notes
  • Invert Y in the input mapping if you want typical inverted mouse behavior; avoid double-negation in code.
  • Clamp pitch using the camera's spring arm or controller constraints to prevent camera flipping.
  • Small sensitivity multipliers can be applied in mapping or before passing to the controller for tuning.
Example
If LookAxisVector.X is 2.0 from input scaling, calling AddControllerYawInput with that value rotates the controller immediately by that delta amount for the frame.

content.html:
Architecture
UFloatingPawnMovement
Create it in the constructor to enable movement handling.
Constructor snippet
// In AMyPlayerPawn.h
#include "GameFramework/FloatingPawnMovement.h"

// In AMyPlayerPawn.cpp constructor
AMyPlayerPawn::AMyPlayerPawn()
{
  UFloatingPawnMovement* FloatingPawnMovement = CreateDefaultSubobject<UFloatingPawnMovement>(TEXT("FloatingPawnMovement"));
  FloatingPawnMovement->MaxSpeed = 1000.0f;
}
Why it matters
  • The movement component processes aggregated AddMovementInput calls into motion and collision response.
  • Setting MaxSpeed gives you a top speed the component enforces.
  • Without it, AddMovementInput may have no visible effect or require custom movement logic.
Safety note
Very high speeds can cause tunneling; test with realistic MaxSpeed and adjust collision thickness or physics if needed.

screens.title: AddMovementInput vs SetActorLocation
screens.narratorSegment: Developers often try to move a pawn by directly setting its location, but that approach sidesteps Unreal's movement and collision systems. SetActorLocation immediately places the actor at a new world position, which can ignore physics responses and produce clipping or tunneling. By contrast, AddMovementInput queues a directional delta that a movement component processes, enabling sliding along collision surfaces and correct collision resolution. For example, moving along a slope with SetActorLocation risks burying the pawn in geometry, while a movement component will slide the pawn along the surface. A common misconception is thinking direct location updates are simpler; they are simpler to code, but they make robust collision handling your responsibility. If you must use SetActorLocation for special cases, call the appropriate collision-swept overloads and handle rejection, but for normal player motion AddMovementInput with a movement component is the safer default. Takeaway: prefer movement requests to ensure predictable collision behavior and smoother gameplay. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

AddMovementInput vs SetActorLocation
Tradeoffs between request-based movement and direct transforms.
AddMovementInput + Component
  • Processed by movement component.
  • Handles sliding and collision.
  • Frame-rate independent when scaled by delta seconds.
SetActorLocation (direct)
  • Immediate position change, bypasses movement pipeline.
  • Risk of clipping/tunneling unless swept collision is used.
  • Requires manual collision and physics handling for robust results.
Pro tip

Choose AddMovementInput for standard player motion; reserve direct location changes for special scripted placements and use swept collision when doing so.

screens.title: Frame-rate independence and GetDeltaSeconds
screens.narratorSegment: Frame-rate independence means the distance a pawn moves per second stays the same regardless of how many frames are rendered in that second. GetWorld()->GetDeltaSeconds() returns the time elapsed since the last frame; using it converts a per-second speed into a per-frame displacement. For example, MovementSpeed set to 500 units per second multiplied by delta seconds of 0.016 yields about 8 units this frame on a 60Hz machine. Without delta seconds, the pawn would move MovementSpeed units every frame and run faster on higher frame rates. A concrete debugging scenario: if your character runs twice as fast on a high-end machine, check for a missing delta seconds multiplier. Another misconception is thinking tick rate alone enforces consistency; tick rate varies with performance and the engine's time management, so explicit multiplication is required. The practical takeaway is to always multiply input-derived scales by GetWorld()->GetDeltaSeconds() when you intend speeds to represent units per second. Frame-rate independence and GetDeltaSeconds means multiply movement scales by getworld()->getdeltaseconds() to convert per-second speeds into correct per-frame displacements.. In practical terms, why multiplying by delta seconds stabilizes movement. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition
Frame-rate independent movement
Why it matters
Speeds should be consistent across devices. Multiply MovementSpeed by GetWorld()->GetDeltaSeconds() so the movement applied each frame equals the fraction of a second passed.
Numeric example
MovementSpeed = 500 units/s. At 60 FPS delta is ~0.016: per-frame move ≈ 8 units. At 30 FPS delta ~0.033: per-frame move ≈ 16 units, but fewer frames keep distance per second consistent.
Common bug & fix
Bug: movement tied to frame rate because code omitted delta seconds. Fix: include GetWorld()->GetDeltaSeconds() when scaling movement input.
Check your code
// Incorrect
AddMovementInput(Forward, InputY * MovementSpeed);

// Correct
AddMovementInput(Forward, InputY * MovementSpeed * GetWorld()->GetDeltaSeconds());

screens.title: Tuning MovementSpeed and MaxSpeed
screens.narratorSegment: Tuning MovementSpeed and the movement component's MaxSpeed is an iterative, playtest-driven process. Start with conservative defaults — the chapter suggests a MovementSpeed of 500 and a FloatingPawnMovement MaxSpeed of 1000 — then play the level to see how the pawn navigates corridors, slopes, and narrow gaps. If you observe tunneling, where the pawn passes through thin geometry, lower the speeds or increase collision thickness and consider enabling swept collision on movement operations. A concrete tuning workflow: set MovementSpeed, run the game at high and low frame rates, confirm consistent coverage per second, and then increase speed until it feels responsive without breaking physics. Also watch responsiveness: a very low speed might feel sluggish even if physically correct. A common misconception is that higher MaxSpeed always improves responsiveness; it can instead lead to less precise collision responses. Takeaway: tune speeds with both collision and feel in mind and test under multiple frame-rate conditions. screens.title: Adapting movement for a top-down game
screens.narratorSegment: The chapter includes an assessment scenario for a top-down game where movement should be relative to the world's axes rather than the controller's look direction. To implement this, replace the controller-derived forward and right vectors with the world's constant axes: use FVector::ForwardVector for world forward and FVector::RightVector for world right. keyIdea.text: Use FVector::ForwardVector and FVector::RightVector in AddMovementInput to move relative to fixed world axes for top-down games.

content.html:
Assessment Scenario
Top-down: world-relative movement
Modified Move
void AMyPlayerPawn::Move(const FInputActionValue& Value)
{
  FVector2D MovementVector = Value.Get<FVector2D>();

  if (Controller && (MovementVector.X != 0.0f || MovementVector.Y != 0.0f))
  {
    const FVector WorldForward = FVector::ForwardVector; // (1,0,0)
    const FVector WorldRight   = FVector::RightVector;   // (0,1,0)

    AddMovementInput(WorldForward, MovementVector.Y * MovementSpeed * GetWorld()->GetDeltaSeconds());
    AddMovementInput(WorldRight,   MovementVector.X * MovementSpeed * GetWorld()->GetDeltaSeconds());
  }
}
Why use it
  • Consistent controls in a fixed-camera top-down view.
  • Movement unaffected by camera rotation.
  • Useful when the camera is canonical, like maps or strategy views.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you'll learn how to turn input axis values into reliable player movement and camera look for an APawn. We'll focus on using Unreal's built-in helpers rather than manually moving actors: AddMovementInput accumulates directional requests and defers to a movement component to handle collision and sliding, while AddControllerYawInput and AddControllerPitchInput update the controller's rotation so the pawn and attached camera follow the player's view. You'll also see why the controller's yaw is used to derive forward and right vectors, and why multiplying by the frame delta is essential to avoid frame-rate dependent speeds. A concrete outcome is a MyPlayerPawn that moves with W/A/S/D, strafes, and looks around with the mouse, with a UFloatingPawnMovement component providing basic physics-aware motion. Along the way we'll highlight common mistakes developers make, such as directly setting actor location or forgetting GetWorld()->GetDeltaSeconds(), and give quick fixes and testing tips. By the end you will be able to implement, tune, and debug basic movement and camera look for a player pawn.

These objectives map to hands-on skills you'll use immediately in your pawn code. First, you'll implement forward, backward, and strafing movement using AddMovementInput so your pawn responds to axis values and respects collision when a movement component is present. Second, you'll wire camera rotation by calling AddControllerYawInput and AddControllerPitchInput so the controller's rotation drives the pawn orientation and any attached spring arm camera. Third, you'll learn the role of AController: it provides GetControlRotation which we use to derive yaw-only forward and right vectors; understanding that relationship prevents common orientation bugs. Fourth, you'll tune movement speed and ensure frame-rate independence by multiplying movement scales by GetWorld()->GetDeltaSeconds(). Each objective includes a brief why and a quick mnemonic to help you test and verify your work. These skills matter because they move you from prototype input logs to a playable pawn that respects physics and feels consistent across machines.

Knowing what to implement is only half the work. This second objectives screen focuses on validating and debugging your movement. You'll test that AddMovementInput produces expected motion by confirming the pawn moves relative to the controller's yaw, and not the world's fixed axes, unless intentionally implemented for a top-down design. You'll check that Look input updates controller rotation and that inverted mouse Y behavior comes from input mapping decisions rather than code. For troubleshooting, learn to reproduce frame-rate variation: simulate a low frame environment and observe whether movement scales correctly — if it doesn't, the fix is to multiply by GetWorld()->GetDeltaSeconds(). Also watch for movement that ignores collision: that usually means no movement component processed the input. Finally, practice tuning MovementSpeed and the movement component's MaxSpeed while watching for tunneling at very high speeds. These validation steps help you move from code changes to a playable, robust pawn.

Start by understanding the division of responsibilities between APawn and AController. The pawn is the in-world actor that can move and collide, but by default it lacks higher-level intent; the controller — often a player controller — provides that intent and the view orientation. GetControlRotation on the controller returns where the player is looking in world space. When we want movement that feels natural to the player, we derive a yaw-only rotation from the controller so the pawn's forward and right directions align with the player's facing direction. This prevents awkward movement where forward on the keyboard moves the pawn in a different direction than the camera. A concrete example: if a player looks 45 degrees right and presses forward, using the controller yaw makes the pawn move toward that 45-degree heading. A common misconception is assuming the pawn's actor rotation always matches the camera. Instead, the controller can be rotated independently; the pawn only follows if you enable bUseControllerRotationYaw or respond to controller rotation explicitly. Takeaway: treat the controller as the source of viewpoint and use its yaw to compute movement axes for player-centric motion.

AddMovementInput is the recommended way to request motion from a pawn. Conceptually, it doesn't instantly teleport the pawn; instead it queues a directional request that a movement component will process. The two main parameters are a world-space FVector direction and a float scale. The direction is typically a unit forward or right vector derived from the controller yaw; the scale comes from your input axis value multiplied by a MovementSpeed and crucially by the frame delta. A concrete example: when the player presses the forward key, the Move function calls AddMovementInput with the derived forward vector and a scale of InputY times MovementSpeed times GetWorld()->GetDeltaSeconds(). A common mistake is to pass raw speed without delta seconds, which ties movement to frame rate. Another pitfall is calling SetActorLocation inside Move — that bypasses collision handling. The right approach is to ensure a UFloatingPawnMovement or character movement component exists to process the queued inputs so sliding and collision work as expected. Takeaway: treat AddMovementInput as a request, and pair it with a movement component. AddMovementInput: parameters and behavior means it queues movement requests processed by a movement component; always scale by delta seconds for consistent motion.. In practical terms, how the function accumulates movement and works with components. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through the Move function implementation used to turn a FVector2D input into forward/back and strafing movement. The implementation begins by extracting the movement vector from the input action value. If there is a valid controller and non-zero input, we get the controller rotation and create a yaw-only rotator to avoid vertical tilt affecting ground movement. Using FRotationMatrix with that yaw produces unit axes: GetUnitAxis(EAxis::X) as forward and GetUnitAxis(EAxis::Y) as right. We then call AddMovementInput twice, one for forward using MovementVector. Y and one for right using MovementVector. X. Each call multiplies by MovementSpeed and GetWorld()->GetDeltaSeconds() so the movement amount represents meters or units per second, independent of frame rate. A concrete example: pressing D yields MovementVector. X positive, causing AddMovementInput with the right vector and moving the pawn to the right relative to the camera. Common pitfalls include forgetting delta seconds or not checking Controller validity. The final check is to confirm a movement component exists so inputs actually move the pawn. Implementing the Move function means derive yaw-only forward/right from controller rotation and call addmovementinput with input axes scaled by movementspeed and delta seconds.. In practical terms, step-by-step c++ example for controller-relative movement. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Camera look is implemented by forwarding mouse or stick input to the controller via AddControllerYawInput and AddControllerPitchInput. These functions change the controller's rotation incrementally, which in turn affects the pawn's orientation if your pawn is set to use controller rotation for yaw or if you read the controller rotation for movement. The Look function should extract a FVector2D look axis from the input action, test controller validity, and call the two functions with the provided X and Y input values. A real example: moving the mouse to the right produces a positive X value; calling AddControllerYawInput with that value rotates the controller right. The chapter mentions negating mouse Y for an inverted look setup, which is controlled via the input mapping rather than code; if your mapping inverts Mouse Y, you do not need to negate again in code. A common mistake is applying pitch directly to the pawn without clamping, which can lead to the camera flipping over. Use your input mapping and spring arm settings to handle clamping and inversion. Final takeaway: keep look input simple — pass values to controller functions and manage inversion in mappings.

AddMovementInput queues movement, but without a movement component nothing may process those requests. UFloatingPawnMovement is a lightweight component you can add in the pawn constructor to provide basic physics-aware motion, MaxSpeed, and collision handling. The chapter suggests creating the component with CreateDefaultSubobject and setting a reasonable MaxSpeed like 1000.0f. A concrete constructor example creates a FloatingPawnMovement subobject and sets MaxSpeed. This component interprets accumulated AddMovementInput calls and applies actual displacement while considering simple collision and sliding. A common pitfall is adding the input calls but forgetting to add the component, producing no visible movement. Another safety note: extremely high MovementSpeed or MaxSpeed can cause tunneling through thin geometry; always test movement at different speeds and adjust collision settings or physics to prevent players getting stuck or falling through. Takeaway: pair AddMovementInput with an appropriate movement component so movement behaves like a first-class physics actor in the world. UFloatingPawnMovement: enabling AddMovementInput means ufloatingpawnmovement processes addmovementinput and provides maxspeed and collision-aware movement; create it in the pawn constructor.. In practical terms, why a movement component is required for collision-aware movement. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Developers often try to move a pawn by directly setting its location, but that approach sidesteps Unreal's movement and collision systems. SetActorLocation immediately places the actor at a new world position, which can ignore physics responses and produce clipping or tunneling. By contrast, AddMovementInput queues a directional delta that a movement component processes, enabling sliding along collision surfaces and correct collision resolution. For example, moving along a slope with SetActorLocation risks burying the pawn in geometry, while a movement component will slide the pawn along the surface. A common misconception is thinking direct location updates are simpler; they are simpler to code, but they make robust collision handling your responsibility. If you must use SetActorLocation for special cases, call the appropriate collision-swept overloads and handle rejection, but for normal player motion AddMovementInput with a movement component is the safer default. Takeaway: prefer movement requests to ensure predictable collision behavior and smoother gameplay. Frame-rate independence means the distance a pawn moves per second stays the same regardless of how many frames are rendered in that second. GetWorld()->GetDeltaSeconds() returns the time elapsed since the last frame; using it converts a per-second speed into a per-frame displacement. For example, MovementSpeed set to 500 units per second multiplied by delta seconds of 0.016 yields about 8 units this frame on a 60Hz machine. Without delta seconds, the pawn would move MovementSpeed units every frame and run faster on higher frame rates. A concrete debugging scenario: if your character runs twice as fast on a high-end machine, check for a missing delta seconds multiplier. Another misconception is thinking tick rate alone enforces consistency; tick rate varies with performance and the engine's time management, so explicit multiplication is required.
